"I think we both had something to learn from each other," he said. "Paul's character had to learn that it's all right to take a little distance from your significant other and have some dude friends and someone to vent to about things you can't necessarily talk about with your girl." "Sometimes buddies hold a mirror up to the way you behave in ways that relationships with the opposite sex don't," Rudd said. "I think that we've all been kind of drawn to real stories, you know, characters that hopefully people can relate to and what's funny about just certain insecurites and just certain things in life. # The Rise of the "Bromance": Rudd and Segel Reflect on Male Friendship On-Screen

**NEW YORK (CNN)** — They've come to be known as "bromances": those buddy films and television shows—think "Pineapple Express" and "The 40-Year-Old Virgin"—that explore deep, platonic friendships between men. The latest entry in this genre, "I Love You, Man," opens Friday and stars Jason Segel and Paul Rudd.

The film follows Paul Rudd's character, Peter Klaven, a man preparing for his wedding who realizes he has no male friends to serve as best man. His search leads him to Sydney Fife, played by Jason Segel, and the two embark on a series of "man-dates" that ultimately put a strain on Peter's relationship with his fiancée, played by Rashida Jones.

Despite the film's obvious fit within the genre, don't dare use the term "bromance" around its stars. "We hate that word," Segel told CNN. Rudd concurred, noting, "It was not part of the lexicon while we were filming."

Nevertheless, both actors bring considerable experience to this particular brand of comedy. Rudd has appeared in numerous films written, directed, or produced by Judd Apatow, widely regarded as a pioneer of the genre for his emotionally candid portrayals of male characters. Segel, too, has collaborated with Apatow—most notably in last year's "Forgetting Sarah Marshall"—and currently stars in the television series "How I Met Your Mother," which mines considerable humor from male camaraderie.

According to Segel, the genre's comedic power lies in the tension of watching two men attempt to navigate emotional vulnerability while clinging to a stoic, traditionally masculine exterior. He's well aware of his particular knack for generating that tension on-screen.

"Judd Apatow told me that my special skill was that I am able to maintain my likability while getting incredibly close to the creepy line, and that's what I should try to cultivate," he explained.

"That's what he does," Rudd affirmed. "He just holds [the moment] a little too long."

"It's the fraction of a second too long that makes people uncomfortable," Segel added.

In "I Love You, Man," Segel's character diverges from the more restrained personas he's played in "Sarah Marshall" and "How I Met Your Mother"—a shift he welcomed. "It was a real treat for me, to be honest for a minute, to play this character, because I've played sort of a puppy dog guy in 'Forgetting Sarah Marshall,' and on ['Mother'] I play a husband, you know, a loving husband," he said. "So to get to play a character who is a bit more of a man of mystery was very exciting for me."

Segel even claims to have his own version of a "man cave" in real life. "It's filled with puppets," he revealed. "And I keep wondering why I don't have a girlfriend. I'm like, 'Hey, this is my house; come check it out. This is where I keep my 40 puppets.'... I think that I have a reputation for being weird because of that."

Turning more serious, Segel insists that beneath its comedic surface, "I Love You, Man" carries a genuine message. "I think we both had something to learn from each other," he said. "Paul's character had to learn that it's all right to take a little distance from your significant other and have some dude friends and someone to vent to about things you can't necessarily talk about with your girl."

"Sometimes buddies hold a mirror up to the way you behave in ways that relationships with the opposite sex don't," Rudd added.

"Yeah, and my character had to learn that maybe it's time to grow up a little bit," Segel said.

So perhaps this "bromance" phenomenon—this willingness to let a few emotions show—isn't such a bad thing after all. Rudd agrees there's merit to the concept, regardless of its label, and expresses satisfaction with its popularity.

"That's us in a nutshell—not macho, not tough," he said. "I think that we've all been kind of drawn to real stories, characters that hopefully people can relate to, and what's funny about certain insecurities and certain things in life."

"They could easily be dramatic," he added with a smile. "Just less fart jokes."

This Friday, moviegoers will get their latest dose of "bromance" with the release of "I Love You, Man," starring Jason Segel and Paul Rudd. The film represents the newest entry in a growing genre that has found its footing in both film and television—one centered on the deep, emotionally resonant, yet entirely non-sexual friendships between men.

## The Plot: A Search for a Best Man

At the heart of the film is Peter Klaven, played by Paul Rudd, a man who finds himself in an unusual predicament: he has no close male friends to speak of. With his wedding fast approaching, Peter faces the awkward reality that he has no one to serve as his best man. This sets him off on a series of increasingly uncomfortable "man-dates," ultimately leading him to Sydney Fife, played by Jason Segel. As Peter and Sydney's friendship blossoms, however, the time and emotional energy Peter invests in this new bond begins to take a toll on his relationship with his fiancée, creating tension between his romantic commitment and his newfound camaraderie.

## Rejecting the "Bromance" Label

Despite starring in a film that seems tailor-made for the bromance genre—and despite their own histories with similar material—both Rudd and Segel have been vocal about their distaste for the term itself. According to the actors, "bromance" simply wasn't part of the conversation or vocabulary on set during filming. They seem wary of reducing their work to a trendy buzzword, preferring instead to let the film's exploration of male friendship speak for itself without the catchy, media-friendly label attached.

## The Apatow Connection

It's worth noting that both actors bring substantial experience to this territory, having worked extensively on projects produced by Judd Apatow. Apatow has become something of a defining figure in modern comedy, credited with popularizing a new archetype: the emotionally open, vulnerable male character who isn't afraid to show sincerity and sentiment amid the laughs. This shift in comedic sensibility—moving away from purely stoic or hyper-masculine portrayals of men—has helped pave the way for films like "I Love You, Man" to find both critical and commercial footing.

## Segel's Comedic Philosophy: Walking the "Creepy Line"

Offering some insight into his own approach to comedy, Segel described a specific technique he relies on to generate laughs while keeping his characters sympathetic. He explained that the key to his comedic success is maintaining audience likability even as he pushes scenes toward what he calls the "creepy line"—that uncomfortable territory where humor and unease intersect. One of his favorite tools for achieving this effect is timing: he'll often hold an emotional moment or a meaningful glance just a fraction of a second longer than what feels natural or comfortable, creating a subtle sense of awkwardness that generates laughs while still keeping the character grounded and relatable.

# "I Love You, Man": Redefining Male Friendship on the Big Screen

Paul Rudd and Jason Segel are at the forefront of what critics and audiences have dubbed the "bromance" genre with their new film "I Love You, Man." The movie follows Peter Klaven (Rudd), a real estate agent who realizes upon his engagement that he has no close male friends—no one to stand as his best man. His search for male companionship leads him to Sydney Fife (Segel), a laid-back, unapologetically himself guy whose friendship with Peter blossoms into something deeper and, at times, hilariously awkward.

Despite the film being categorized as a quintessential "bromance," both Rudd and Segel have pushed back against the label. "I don't even know what that word means anymore," Rudd has said in interviews, suggesting that the term oversimplifies what the film is actually trying to explore: the complicated, often unspoken rules governing male friendship and emotional expression.

That complexity is precisely where the film finds its comedic gold. "I Love You, Man" mines humor from the very real discomfort many men feel when confronted with vulnerability, especially in front of other men. Peter's fumbling attempts to bond with Sydney—awkward hangouts, mistimed compliments, and cringe-worthy attempts at male bonding rituals—capture a universal male anxiety about appearing too soft, too needy, or too emotionally open.

Segel, who has built a career playing endearingly unfiltered characters, says achieving the right comedic tone requires a delicate balancing act. "There's a fine line between funny-awkward and just plain creepy," he has explained, describing his approach to the role. "I try to push scenes right up to that edge of creepy without ever actually crossing it. That's where the real comedy lives—in that uncomfortable space where you're not sure if a moment is sweet or slightly unsettling."

This tension—between traditional masculine stoicism and genuine emotional connection—reflects a broader shift happening in American comedy. Producer Judd Apatow, whose fingerprints (thematically, if not always literally) can be seen across this wave of male-centered films, has long championed stories that allow men to be emotionally messy, insecure, and vulnerable while still being funny and relatable. Films in this vein tend to explore friendship, loyalty, and identity among men in ways that mainstream comedy had largely avoided in previous decades, favoring instead a more macho, emotionally guarded archetype.

"I Love You, Man" fits squarely within this evolving landscape, using the framework of a wedding-adjacent buddy comedy to ask deeper questions about what it means for men to form authentic friendships in a culture that often discourages emotional openness. Whether or not audiences and critics settle on "bromance" as the definitive term for this genre, the film taps into something many viewers recognize: the awkward, sometimes painfully funny process of learning to let another person in.

# Paul Rudd and Jason Segel Talk 'Bromance' Ahead of New Comedy

**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — Paul Rudd and Jason Segel are used to playing best friends on screen, but their new film "I Love You, Man" pushes the concept to new, hilariously awkward heights — and the two stars say they couldn't be happier to be at the center of what's being called the "bromance" boom.

The film, which opens in theaters this Friday, follows Rudd's character Peter Klaven, a socially awkward real estate agent who realizes he has no close male friends as he prepares to marry his girlfriend. Enter Segel's Sydney Fife, a laid-back, free-spirited guy who becomes Peter's best man — and the object of what can only be described as a full-blown, non-romantic courtship.

"It's basically a romantic comedy, except instead of falling in love with a girl, I fall in love with a dude," Rudd said with a laugh during a press day interview. "The stakes are still there. The awkward first hangout, the 'will he text me back' anxiety — it's all the same beats, just between two guys."

Segel, best known for his role on "How I Met Your Mother" and his breakout in "Forgetting Sarah Marshall," said he was drawn to the script because it captured something real about adult male friendships that rarely gets explored on screen.

"Guys don't really talk about how hard it is to make friends as an adult," Segel said. "You have all these buddies in high school and college, and then suddenly you're 30 and you realize you don't actually know how to make a new friend. It's genuinely awkward, and I think that's what makes it funny — because it's true."

Both actors pushed back slightly on the term "bromance" itself, even as they acknowledged its cultural staying power.

"I don't hate the word, but I do think it undersells what these relationships actually are," Rudd said. "Some of the most important relationships in my life are with my guy friends. It's not a joke — it's just that nobody had a good word for it before, so now we're stuck with 'bromance.'"

Segel agreed, adding that the genre — which has included everything from "Superbad" to "Pineapple Express" — resonates because audiences are hungry to see male friendship portrayed with real emotional stakes, not just as a backdrop to a romantic plot.

"There's vulnerability in it," he said. "Peter has to be honest about the fact that he's lonely and he wants a friend. That's not something you usually see a male character admit on screen. I think audiences respond to that honesty, even inside a broad comedy."

The film also stars Rashida Jones as Peter's fiancée, along with Jon Favreau, Jaime Pressly and J.K. Simmons rounding out the supporting cast. Director John Hamburg, who co-wrote "Meet the Parents" and "Zoolander," said he wanted the film to feel grounded despite its comedic premise.

Rudd and Segel, who had never worked together before this project, said their off-screen chemistry developed quickly — ironically mirroring the very friendship arc their characters go through in the film.

"By the second week of shooting, we were basically finishing each other's sentences," Segel said. "Which, now that I say it out loud, sounds exactly like the plot of the movie."

"I Love You, Man" opens in theaters nationwide March 20.

# Comedy's Odd Couple: Jason Segel and Paul Rudd on Bromance, Vulnerability, and Why Men Need Better Scripts for Friendship

*A fictional interview*

---

The coffee shop in Los Feliz is nearly empty on a Tuesday morning, which is probably why Jason Segel picked it. He arrives first, folds his six-foot-four frame into a corner booth, and orders black coffee. Paul Rudd shows up twelve minutes later, apologizing for traffic that doesn't quite explain the delay, and orders the same.

They've known each other for almost two decades, since a small role brought Rudd into Segel's orbit during the Apatow years. What follows is a conversation that meanders from their early collaborations to something more unguarded: how comedy became the language through which they, and a generation of male performers, learned to talk about friendship at all.

---

**On how they met and what clicked:**

**RUDD:** I remember thinking, this guy is going to make me look bad by being taller and funnier. That's not a great combination to walk into a scene with.

**SEGEL:** What actually happened is we were both terrified. Everyone assumes there's this effortless chemistry, but the truth is comedy between two guys works when you're both willing to look like an idiot first. I think we clocked that in each other pretty early. Paul will just commit to something humiliating without flinching.

**RUDD:** Thank you? I think that's a compliment.

---

**On why "bromance" became such a durable genre:**

**SEGEL:** I've always thought the word itself is a little bit of a cop-out, honestly. It lets everyone off the hook. Like, we can show two men who genuinely love each other, who are vulnerable with each other, but we have to slap this jokey label on it so nobody gets uncomfortable.

**RUDD:** Right, it's a permission slip.

**SEGEL:** Exactly. But underneath the permission slip, something real is happening. I think a lot of guys watched those movies and it was the first time they'd seen male friendship depicted with any emotional stakes at all. Usually men on screen are just cracking jokes past each other. We tried to write scripts where the jokes were the Trojan horse for something sincere.

**RUDD:** I don't think we always succeeded, by the way.

**SEGEL:** No, definitely not always.

---

**On vulnerability and the fear of sincerity:**

**RUDD:** There's a specific terror in comedy of playing a scene straight. You do a take that's actually emotionally honest and everyone on set gets quiet, and your instinct is to immediately make a joke to break the tension you just created.

**SEGEL:** That instinct is the whole problem, though. That's the same instinct guys have in real friendships. Something real starts to surface and the joke comes in like a fire extinguisher.

**RUDD:** So what do you do?

**SEGEL:** You let the take breathe. I had to learn that. Judd [Apatow] used to just leave the camera rolling past the point where I was comfortable, and something else would show up. Usually something sadder and more true than the joke I was reaching for.

---

**On what's changed in how they write and play male friendship:**

**RUDD:** I think we ask characters to say "I love you" now in ways that would have felt impossible fifteen years ago. Not as a punchline setup necessarily, though it can still be funny. But as just... true.

**SEGEL:** I care about that a lot, actually. I have friends, guys my age, who still cannot say a sincere sentence to another man without immediately undercutting it. And I understand why. I do it too, probably right now in this conversation.

**RUDD:** You're doing pretty well right now.

**SEGEL:** Give it time.

*(Both laugh)*

**SEGEL:** But I think comedy has quietly done more to model emotional honesty between men than almost any other genre, because it sneaks in under the joke. Audiences let their guard down for a laugh, and then suddenly there's a scene where two guys are actually talking, actually saying the hard thing, and nobody feels like they've wandered into a lecture.

**RUDD:** That's the trick, yeah. Nobody wants the lecture. They want the friend.

---

**On advice for the next generation of comedic duos:**

**RUDD:** Be willing to lose. In a scene, in a friendship. Whoever's most afraid to look bad usually is.

**SEGEL:** And don't confuse the joke for the point. The joke's the delivery system. What you're actually trying to say is usually something a lot more tender than the joke lets on.

**RUDD:** Says the six-foot-four man who once cried in a Muppet costume on camera.

**SEGEL:** *(laughing)* That was a great day at work, actually.

# "I Love You, Man" Hits Theaters, Cast Credits Apatow's Comedy Empire for Career Boosts

**LOS ANGELES** — The bromance comedy "I Love You, Man" opened in theaters this weekend, bringing star Paul Rudd's everyman charm to a leading role as Peter Klaven, a socially awkward real estate agent who embarks on a series of disastrous "man-dates" to find a best friend before his wedding. Co-starring Jason Segel as the loose-cannon buddy who fits the bill, the film has drawn comparisons to the wave of R-rated comedies that redefined the genre over the past several years — many of them produced or directed by Judd Apatow.

While Apatow has no direct involvement in "I Love You, Man," the film's DNA is unmistakably shaped by the comedy landscape he helped build with hits like "The 40-Year-Old Virgin," "Knocked Up," and "Forgetting Sarah Marshall." Both lead actors spoke openly about how their association with Apatow's projects changed the trajectory of their careers.

"Before Judd, I was the guy who showed up in a movie for two scenes and then disappeared," Rudd said at the film's press day. "Working with him taught me that comedy could come from being vulnerable and a little pathetic, not just from being the funny best friend cracking one-liners. That's basically the entire character of Peter Klaven right there."

Segel, who broke through with his role in Apatow-produced "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" — for which he also wrote the screenplay — echoed similar sentiments.

"Judd gave me a shot when nobody else would let me carry a movie, let alone write one," Segel said. "He has this philosophy of finding the truth in embarrassing situations and just sitting in that discomfort until it becomes funny. I don't think I make a movie like this without going through that experience first."

Director John Hamburg, who co-wrote "Meet the Parents" and "Zoolander" before stepping behind the camera for "I Love You, Man," acknowledged the influence directly, noting that Apatow's success gave studios newfound confidence in character-driven, R-rated comedies that don't rely on slapstick or gross-out gags alone.

"Five years ago, a studio might have looked at this script and asked, 'Where are the bigger jokes? Where's the wackier stuff?'" Hamburg said. "Judd proved audiences want to laugh at real, awkward human behavior. He kind of cleared a path for movies like this to get made and, more importantly, to get seen."

Rudd, who has become something of an unofficial ensemble player in the loose collective of actors and filmmakers surrounding Apatow, added a lighter note about the community's camaraderie.

"Everyone kind of knows everyone at this point," Rudd laughed. "You do one of Judd's movies, or a movie with people who've done Judd's movies, and suddenly you're at the same barbecues, the same poker games. It's less a career path and more like being drafted into a very funny fraternity."

"I Love You, Man" also stars Rashida Jones, Jaime Pressly, and Jon Favreau, and features a supporting performance from Lou Ferrigno playing an exaggerated version of himself. Early reviews have praised the chemistry between Rudd and Segel, with several critics noting the film's willingness to explore male friendship with the same emotional honesty Apatow's projects have brought to romantic relationships.

Whether or not "I Love You, Man" becomes a box office hit, its existence — and the frank acknowledgment from its stars of Apatow's outsized influence — underscores how thoroughly one filmmaker's sensibility has reshaped what mainstream studio comedy looks like heading into the next decade.

# The Rise of the 'Bromance': Hollywood's Latest Love Story Isn't Between a Man and a Woman

*By a CNN.com Staff Writer*

There's a new kind of love story dominating multiplexes these days, and it doesn't involve a wedding dress or a grand romantic gesture toward a leading lady. Instead, it's about two guys, an awkward first hangout, and the very real anxiety of making a new best friend as an adult.

Welcome to the era of the "bromance" film — and few movies capture the genre's charm quite like "I Love You, Man," starring Paul Rudd and Jason Segel.

The film follows Peter Klaven (Rudd), a newly engaged real estate agent who realizes he has no close male friends to serve as his best man. What follows is a series of "man-dates" that feel eerily similar to romantic courtship — nervous small talk, awkward silences, and the giddy relief of finally clicking with someone.

"It really is like dating," Rudd said in a recent interview promoting the film. "You're sitting there thinking, 'Did I talk too much? Should I text him? Is it too soon to text him?' It's ridiculous how much that mirrors actual romantic relationships, except instead of flowers, you're bonding over Rush concert tickets."

Segel, who plays Sydney Fife — the effortlessly cool, socially unfiltered guy who becomes Peter's unlikely best friend — says the film taps into something real about male friendship that Hollywood has largely ignored.

"Guys don't really have a good model for how to make friends as adults," Segel explained. "When you're a kid, you just go up to someone on a playground and say, 'Hey, wanna be friends?' As an adult, that's basically illegal. So this movie is kind of about relearning how to do that, except with more beer and less finger-painting."

## A Genre Takes Shape

"I Love You, Man" joins a growing list of films — from "Superbad" to "Pineapple Express" — that explore male friendship with the same emotional stakes typically reserved for romantic comedies. Critics have noted that these films often follow a strikingly familiar structure: the meet-cute, the falling out, the tearful reconciliation.

Segel, no stranger to comedic vulnerability after his breakout role in "Forgetting Sarah Marshall," says the comparison to romance isn't an accident.

"Honestly, falling for a friend is just as scary as falling for a partner," he said. "Maybe scarier, because there's no ambiguity about what a first kiss means, but there's a lot of ambiguity about whether it's weird to tell your guy friend you love him. Spoiler: it's not weird. Or maybe it is. We'll let the audience decide."

Rudd, for his part, believes the appeal lies in audiences — especially men — finally seeing their own friendships reflected on screen without irony or shame.

"There's something freeing about being able to say, 'I love this guy,' about your best friend without it being a joke," Rudd said. "Well, it's still kind of a joke in our movie. But it's a joke with heart."

## The Verdict

Whether "bromance" becomes a lasting genre or simply a moment in comedic filmmaking remains to be seen. But if "I Love You, Man" is any indication, audiences are more than ready to watch two grown men navigate friendship with the same nervous energy — and the same emotional payoff — as any great love story.

As Segel put it: "At the end of the day, isn't that just what a great friendship is? A slightly less physical romance with better snacks?"

"I Love You, Man" is now playing in theaters nationwide.

# The Bromance Boys: Rudd and Segel Talk Man-Dates, Man-Crushes, and Man-Hugs

There's a moment in "I Love You, Man" where Paul Rudd's character, Peter Klaven, tries to master a complicated handshake-hug combo with his new best friend Sydney Fife, played by Jason Segel. It goes horribly, comically wrong—all elbows and awkward timing. It's a scene that could serve as a metaphor for the entire genre that's sprung up around the film: the "bromance," a term Hollywood has embraced with the enthusiasm of a guy who just discovered he and his buddy have the same fantasy football strategy.

Sitting down with Rudd and Segel, it's clear neither actor set out to make a defining entry in a movement. They just wanted to make a funny movie about something rarely discussed on screen: adult male friendship, and how genuinely strange and vulnerable it is to make a new friend as a grown man.

"Nobody sat us down and said, 'Okay, this is the bromance,'" Rudd said, laughing. "We were just trying to tell a story about a guy who doesn't have any close friends because he's spent his whole adult life orienting his life around girlfriends. That's a real thing. I've met people like that."

Segel, never one to resist a tangent, jumped in. "I definitely went through a phase where all my friends were 'my girlfriend's friends' who I inherited. You get real good at pretending to like people's brothers."

The film's premise—Peter, freshly engaged, realizes he has no groomsmen prospects and embarks on a series of disastrous "man-dates" before hitting it off with the blunt, Rush-obsessed Sydney—was, according to both actors, mined from real embarrassment.

"I've been on man-dates," Rudd admitted. "Not called that, obviously, but that terrifying thing where you meet a guy, you like him, and you don't know the etiquette. Do you hug? Do you text him first? Is it weird if you text him first?"

"It's exactly like dating," Segel said. "Except if it goes wrong, you can't even cry about it to your friends, because the whole problem is you don't have any."

As for the term "bromance" itself, both actors have a sort of amused détente with it.

"I don't hate it," Segel said, shrugging. "It's better than some of the other words they could've come up with. Could be worse. They could call it 'himance.' 'Guyance.'"

Rudd was a little more skeptical. "I think what's funny is that the word makes it sound like a genre, like it's a niche thing, when really it's just... friendship. Movies have never had a problem showing two guys shoot each other or blow things up together. But two guys being emotionally honest? That's somehow the wild concept."

He paused. "Although I will say, doing press for this movie, I've hugged Jason more in the last three weeks than I've hugged anyone in years. So maybe the term is accurate."

Segel nodded solemnly. "We've become an actual bromance making a movie about a fake one. It's very meta. It's like method acting, except the method is texting each other 'miss you man' unironically."

The two have an easy chemistry that clearly extended off-camera. During filming, they said, much of Peter and Sydney's dynamic—including an improvised riff about slang terms for vomiting that became a standout scene—came from just letting the tape roll and seeing what happened.

"We did probably forty minutes of just synonyms for throwing up," Segel said. "Judd [Apatow, a producer] loves that. He'll just let you go until you've exhausted every possible joke, and then keep going past that."

"There's a version of this movie that's three hours long and it's just me and Jason inventing words," Rudd added. "The studio would not have loved that cut."

Both actors pushed back gently on the idea that "I Love You, Man" is somehow only "for guys." Rudd noted that some of the most enthusiastic responses in test screenings came from women who related to Peter's fiancée, played by Rashida Jones, watching her partner navigate this bizarre, tender process of trying to make a friend.

"It's a relationship movie," Rudd said. "It's just that the relationship happens to not have kissing in it. Well—" he stopped. "Actually, there might be a hug that goes on a little too long."

"There's a slow-mo hug," Segel confirmed. "We shot it very romantically. Lots of hair-blowing-in-wind energy."

As for whether they'd sign on for more "bromance" fare, both seemed happy to let the label be someone else's problem.

"I don't think you chase a genre," Rudd said. "You just try to make something true, and if people want to put a word on it, that's on them. Although," he added, glancing at Segel, "if we do a sequel, I do think we've earned the right to design our own handshake. A really good one. Ten seconds, minimum."

Segel grinned. "I've already got ideas. It involves a spin."

Whatever the term ends up meaning long-term—whether "bromance" becomes a permanent fixture of the cultural lexicon or fades as quickly as it arrived—Rudd and Segel seem less concerned with defining a movement than with the simpler pleasure of having made something that, at its core, is about two people (of the male, platonic-friendship variety) figuring out how to let someone in.

"At the end of the day," Rudd said, "it's a movie about being honest with someone else, which is scary no matter your gender. We just happened to put a Rush concert in it."

"I Love You, Man" is now playing in theaters.
